formNote: Mojidata IDS: ⿹气米. The Shuowen distinguishes 气, 雲气也, “cloud vapour”, from 氣, 饋客芻米也, “fodder and rice given to guests”. The graph for the gift was borrowed for the word for vapour.
summary: Breath, vapour, the stuff of life: in early Chinese thought, what condenses into things and disperses at death. Its graph once meant rice given to guests; in Japanese it is ki, in Korean gi.
placement: At the origin, a fixed point of the system near the centre of the three lobes: the qi that the whole flow turns around. (Placement is a design choice, not a claim.)

oc.note: † Baracus, from general knowledge; not yet checked against B–S 2014.

satellites.title: Vapour, and Rice for Guests
satellites.evidence: The Shuowen has two entries: 气，雲气也, “cloud vapour”, and 氣，饋客芻米也, “fodder and rice given to guests”, with 米 in it (Mojidata IDS: ⿹气米). The word for breath came to be written with the graph for a meal shared.

satellites.title: Life Is the Gathering of Qi
satellites.evidence: Zhuangzi ch. 22: 人之生，氣之聚也；聚則為生，散則為死 — “a person’s life is the gathering of qi; gathered, it is life; scattered, it is death.” Birth and death as one substance condensing and dispersing.

satellites.title: Breath as Life, Elsewhere
satellites.evidence: Greek πνεῦμα (wind, breath, spirit) and Sanskrit prāṇa (breath, the life-force) also make breath the stuff of life. Three traditions, without contact at the start, reached for the air moving in a body.
satellites.caveat: An analogy: the three concepts differ in their systems (qi also makes up rocks and weather), and none renders the others in early texts.
